Roman Republic, Cn. Lentulus AR Denarius, 74 BC. Minted to pay Pompey's legions during the Sertorian war

In 80 BC, a revolt broke out in the Roman province of Hispania(modern-day Spain) led by a Roman general named Quintus Sertorius who was attempting to keep his head on his shoulders after having supported the losing side in some recent violent political upheaval in Rome. Sertorius and his Roman troops allied themselves with a local Iberian tribe known as the Lusitani who were also seeking independence and began fighting against Roman rule in the region. Rome sent in the general Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius to quell the revolt and the conflict quickly became Rome's first big encounter with guerrilla tactics which Metellus was not at all prepared to handle.

In 77 BC, Rome sent in the young upshot general Pompey(who we now know as Pompey Magnus("The Great") for a reason) to help Metellus put down the revolt. Even with the additional troops and tactics of Pompey, however, Rome was still having trouble subduing Sertorius and his rebels. In 74 BC, a broke and tired Pompey wrote a letter to the senate, which is recorded in Sallust's "Histories" in which he argued that Rome must send money to pay the troops, and that so far he's paid them out of his own pocket, but that he's only been able to pay them for one year of the three they've been fighting. Pompey also warned that, should Rome ignore his call for aid, his own soldiers might revolt and come for Rome itself. Being sensible people who knew all about the importance of paying soldiers, the Senate decreed that an issue of coinage be made to pay Pompey's soldiers and that's where this particular one comes in.

This issue was minted in 74 BC at an unknown Spanish mint, most likely one traveling with the troops, under the quaestor(a financial/treasury official) Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus under the authority of the senate. The figure on the obverse is the "GENIO POPVLI ROMANI" or "Genius of the Roman People", abbreviated "GPR", which is a sort of abstract figure representing the essence of the people of Rome. The meaning of the reverse imagery is not immediately apparent, but we do know that the text "EX SC" basically means "From a decree of the senate", further supporting the fact that this was the issue from the Senate recorded by Sallust. The text below it, "CN LEN Q" is a reference to the fact that it was minted by Cn. Lentulus, Quaestor.

Back to the history though, even with the payment, Pompey and his armies were still having trouble countering Sertorius's guerrilla tactics and the war dragged on. Luckily for Pompey and Metellus, in 72 BC a rival military leader, Marcus Perpenna Vento, assassinated Sertorius and attempted to take control of the late general's legions for himself. Unfortunately for Perpenna, he was not the tactician that Sertorius was and Pompey was able to quickly subdue him and in usual Roman fashion, had him executed shortly thereafter, ending the conflict.

The war is notable for the fact that it forced Rome to really study and adapt against guerrilla tactics. Additionally, this was a huge milestone in the career and popularity of Pompey who quickly became known as one of the greatest military leaders Rome had ever seen, and his victories in Hispania lead to his first triumph, a sort of parade through the streets celebrating military victory.

Full ID: Roman Republic, Cn. Lentulus, AR Denarius(3.9g, 19mm, 6h). 74 BC. Spanish(?) mint. Obverse: Male bust right(Genius Populi Romani), draped hair tied with band, and with sceptre over shoulder; above, G P R. Border of dots. Reverse: Sceptre with wreath, globe and rudder; on left, EX; on right, S C; below, CN LEN Q. Border of dots. Crawford 393/1a. Cornelia 54. Sydenham 752.
